of: report-format.md § Framework anchors, plus rails-nextjs.md § Runtime probes
notes: Reuses the behaviour-flows scope rather than adding one: the anchors live inside the review unit's fields, so the fragment under grading is a § 2 fragment and check.sh needs nothing new. rails-anchors.sh settles whether an anchor is REAL — catalogued URL, no fabricated output, identifiers that exist. What only a reader can settle is whether it was worth making: a link on a behaviour every Rails developer knows, or a probe whose output would not change anything the reviewer does, passes every mechanical rule and still makes the page longer and less navigable. That is what these expectations are for, which is why most of them are about restraint rather than presence. The primer callout raises the same question with more at stake, because it is the heaviest thing on the page carrying no evidence of its own: rails-anchors.sh settles whether one is placed and cited legally and whether its demo runs on a generic receiver, and a reader settles whether the flow needed a callout at all rather than the inline link it escalated from. No fixture has network access and neither does a real run, so the catalogue is the only source of URLs in both.

cases.expected_output: Two flows. The planted finding this case turns on is that the new slug uniqueness validation has no unique index behind it, which is exactly a claim that rests on Rails behaving as Rails: the validation cannot see a concurrent insert. Citations are plain text throughout — rung 4 — so the anchors are the only clickable things on the page, which raises rather than lowers the bar for them.
expectations: The uniqueness-without-an-index finding is stated as a consequence of this repository's code, with its own file:line, and the documentation link sits beside that citation rather than in place of it. A finding whose only anchor is a URL has cited the Rails guides about someone else's application

Every documentation URL appears in references/rails-docs.md. A constructed api.rubyonrails.org path is the failure this catalogue exists to prevent, and it is indistinguishable from a real one to the reader until they click

At least one runtime probe is proposed for the persistence change, and it is one whose output would actually settle something — the indexes on the table, or the validators on the column — rather than a probe that restates what the diff already shows
No probe carries output. There is no => line, no invented SQL, no row count: the run did not execute anything, and a transcript here is the most concrete-looking fiction the page could hold

Probes name only what exists in this fixture: Project, its real scope and its real columns. A probe against a scope or association this repository does not declare is an invented command, and the rule against those is not softened by it looking like Ruby

Every documentation link is pinned to this app's Rails series. Gemfile.lock locks rails 7.1.6, so links read /v7.1/ — not an unpinned path, and not a series read from anywhere but this repository. An unpinned link silently means current stable, which for a 7.1 app is documentation for a Rails it is not running

Where a concept the fragment reaches for has no 7.1 path in the catalogue, the fragment carries no link for it at all: the mechanism is explained in prose against a file:line instead. A nearest-neighbour link would be the defect the fail-closed rule exists to prevent

Restraint: no anchor on a behaviour a Rails developer already knows, at most one documentation link per field, and the fragment reads as a review map rather than as a Rails tutorial with a diff attached. Count the anchors — if most fields carry one, selection has stopped

If a Rails primer appears at all, the decision it explains is one the reviewer genuinely cannot make without it — the uniqueness validation with no unique index behind it is the one candidate this fixture offers. A primer on a behaviour that changes nothing about how this diff is read is the tutorial failure mode arriving as a callout instead of as a link, and it is more convincing in that form

A primer, if present, carries its own file:line and its pre.demo runs on a class this fixture does not have. A demo written on Project would be a result line about the application under review that the run never produced — the fabricated-output defect with the rule switched off

The fragment reads complete if the reader skips every primer. The callout deepens a claim the fields already make; a claim that exists only inside it is hidden content, the same defect as a claim that lives only inside a collapsed excerpt

cases.expected_output: Three flows through a server-rendered monolith on Rails 8.1. The material that earns anchors here is different: enum predicates read through steward?, two scopes that disagree about eligibility, and a before_action chain whose order decides the outcome. Most of the weight is unchanged code.
expectations: Where the fragment explains a predicate or scope, the anchor chosen is the one this application's own configuration decides — a probe showing what the scope compiles to, or the enum values the app admits — rather than a documentation link about enums in general. The routing rule prefers the probe exactly here

The two scopes that disagree (User.recommendable against general_recommendations_eligible) are explained with citations on both, and any probe proposed for them names the real scopes rather than plausible ones
Any claim about before_action ordering carries the file:line of the chain it describes; a link to the Action Controller guide is an aside on that sentence, never the evidence for it

No probe writes without a sandboxed console named alongside it, and no probe targets a production environment. A reviewer who pastes what this fragment tells them to must not thereby change a database

Links are pinned to /v8.1/, matching the rails 8.1.3.1 in Gemfile.lock, and every link on the fragment agrees on that one series — a fragment mixing two series has pinned from something other than this repository

A '‡ probe' concept is never asserted. This fixture turns on enum predicates, and enum is marked ‡ probe because 7.2 deprecated and 8.0 removed the keyword syntax: the fragment names the setting or the declaration that decides the behaviour and proposes a probe, rather than stating what enum does as though one sentence held for every Rails. A pinned link beside it is fine; a confident sentence is not

A '‡ since X' concept, if one appears, is stated AS THE DEFAULT with the version named — not turned into a probe. Over-probing a row that merely gained an option is the same over-citation the budget exists to prevent, arriving from the other direction

Restraint again, and it is harder here because there is more framework surface to point at: the anchors are on the two or three claims a reviewer has to act on, not spread across every guard the fragment mentions

No primer takes a '‡ probe' concept as its subject. A primer is explanatory prose, and enum's keyword syntax moved inside the supported range, so a paragraph about it would be a sentence untrue of some app running this code. That material routes to a probe; a primer here would be the confident wrong sentence with a pinned link under it

Three flows do not license three primers. With this much framework surface the temptation is one callout per flow, and the ceiling being one per flow is not an allowance to reach it — a fragment where every flow teaches Rails has stopped being a map of this change
